title: Georgia Seller's Property Disclosure Statement
description: Georgia law does not mandate a specific form, but the GAR Seller's Property Disclosure (F220) is the industry standard. Sellers must disclose known material defects.

required_actions.note: No state-mandated form. GAR F220 is standard.

title: BRRETA Agency Disclosure
description: Georgia BRRETA requires agents to disclose their agency relationship at first meaningful contact. Buyer/Seller Brokerage Agreements must be in writing.

title: Georgia Real Estate Transfer Tax
description: Georgia imposes a real estate transfer tax of $1.00 for the first $1,000 of consideration (or fractional part) plus $0.10 for each additional $100 (or fractional part) — effectively 0.1% — on transfers where consideration exceeds $100. The seller (grantor executing the deed) is legally liable, though contracts often shift it to the buyer. The tax is paid to the clerk of superior court when the deed is recorded and must be accompanied by an electronically filed Form PT-61 submitted through the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority (GSCCCA).

required_actions.note: E-file PT-61 Real Estate Transfer Tax Declaration via GSCCCA; tax paid to clerk of superior court at recording.
Rate: $1.00 per first $1,000 + $0.10 per additional $100 (~0.1%). Seller is statutorily liable under O.C.G.A. §48-6-3.

title: Attorney-Required Closing State
description: Georgia is an attorney closing state. The Supreme Court of Georgia has held that it is the unauthorized practice of law for anyone other than a Georgia-licensed attorney to close a real estate transaction or to prepare and facilitate the execution of deeds of conveyance. The attorney must be physically present at the closing and may not merely telephonically supervise a non-lawyer (no 'mail-away' or witness-only closings supervised remotely).

required_actions.note: A Georgia-licensed attorney must conduct the closing and be physically present; preparing/facilitating the deed by a non-lawyer is UPL.

citations: In re UPL Advisory Opinion No. 2003-2, 277 Ga. 472 (2003)

title: No Duty to Disclose Psychologically Impacted Property
description: Under O.C.G.A. §44-1-16, no cause of action arises against an owner or broker for failing to disclose that a property was the site of a homicide, felony, suicide, or death by any means, or was occupied by a person infected with a disease (e.g., HIV) not transmitted by occupancy. A buyer may make a written inquiry about such facts; the licensee should consult the owner and respond in good faith but is not obligated to volunteer the information.

required_actions.note: Stigma facts (death, felony, disease) need not be volunteered; respond in good faith only to a written buyer inquiry after consulting the owner.

metadata.note: This is a safe-harbor / no-duty rule, not an affirmative disclosure obligation.
